points.en: The story is not a container or decoration for the message; the story itself is the message, the vehicle that carries truth into the heart.
Facts may convince the mind, but a story moves the heart, where decisions are made.
Explains why each matters: the first frees the preacher to use stories as real preaching, the second shows information alone often changes nothing.
Supports the ideas with Jesus' practice or Nathan and David.
Jesus answered 'What is God like?' with three stories (lost sheep, lost coin, lost son), not a lecture or points about lostness.
All three make one point: God is a seeker who does not rest until the lost is found.
The preacher should likewise show God through story, since narrative carries truth about God more powerfully than abstract propositions.
Notes that the common people heard Jesus gladly (Mark 12:37).
Retells: David hid adultery and murder; Nathan told of a rich man who took a poor man's only ewe lamb, David condemned him, and Nathan said 'Thou art the man.'
Nathan used a story because David already knew the facts and held power; he had to be reached through the heart, not merely informed.
Connecting means putting together things that seemed unrelated so the hearer gains a new, personal insight into his own life.
Identifies the figures: Bathsheba the ewe lamb, David the rich man, Uriah the poor man.
Concedes that a story can be misused as entertainment, yet misuse does not make the method wrong.
Jesus characteristically preached in stories, and no one can say he failed to preach the Word, so a story can carry the full weight of truth.
The real test is whether the story carries the truth of God, not story versus substance.
Distinguishes abuse (entertainment for its own sake) from right use (conveying a biblical truth).
Flesch found two factors make writing interesting: personal words (I, we, you, personal names) and personal stories; people like stories about people.
Gives two concrete, realistic applications for a sermon, such as naming characters, addressing hearers as 'you', or replacing an abstract point with a personal story.
Keeps the aim on conveying truth rather than mere interest.
Every sermon must be faithful to Scripture, but sermon form (expository, topical, narrative) is a separate matter, so not every sermon must be expository.
Narrative preaching is a biblical form: it draws its substance from the Word and can be wholly faithful without going verse by verse.
Appeals to Jesus' parables as proof that a non-expository form can be fully biblical.
A preacher known as dull gave his testimony and became animated and interesting, yet his traditional sermon lost the room.
It shows the power lies in the form of the story, not the man's eloquence: stories engage the hearer and carry a vitality that abstraction lacks.
Connects it to the principle that people like stories about people.
Takes and defends a clear position on whether preaching aims at visions rather than reasons.
Supports it from Scripture, for example Nathan's ewe lamb, Jesus' parables or the prophets' pictures, which moved hearers to see and respond.
Notes that visions do not replace truth but carry it to the heart, so the sermon still proclaims the Word.
Mandate: since Jesus characteristically taught in stories, the preacher should use story as a legitimate, powerful biblical form and not despise it.
Limit: the story must carry the truth of God and not entertain for its own sake.
Limits: the story must be honest and well-sourced, not embellished or stolen, and must serve the text rather than replace it.
Chooses one Christian doctrine and sketches a concrete story, biblical or contemporary, that could carry it instead of a lecture.
States clearly the truth the story must land, keeping the story subordinate to that truth.
Avoids a story that merely entertains without teaching.
